context: A ball is released at the top of a slope and rolls to the bottom. The graph of s(t) shows the distance, in metres, that the ball still has to roll, t seconds after it is released. The graph is a straight line from (0, L) to (T, 0).
stem: A ball is released at the top of a ${=L}$ m slope and rolls to the bottom. The graph of $s(t)$ shows the distance, in metres, that the ball still has to roll, $t$ seconds after it is released. The graph is a straight line that starts at the point $(0, {=L})$ and ends at the point $({=T}, 0)$. After how many seconds has the ball rolled ${=r}$ m?
solution: The graph shows the distance still to roll, not the distance already rolled. When the ball has rolled ${=r}$ m it still has ${=L} - {=r} = {=rem}$ m to roll, so we need the time $t$ at which $s(t) = {=rem}$.
The line goes from $(0, {=L})$ to $({=T}, 0)$, so the ball covers ${=L}$ m in ${=T}$ s, which is ${=q}$ s for every metre it rolls.
The ball has rolled ${=r}$ m, so $t = {=r} \times {=q} = {=ans}$ s. Check: the point $({=ans}, {=rem})$ is on the line, because the ball then still has ${=rem}$ m to roll.
notes: Reads the book's ball graph (ex6-1-8a) in the opposite direction: given an output-side fact, find the time. The twist is that s(t) is the distance still to roll but the question asks about the distance already rolled; a learner who reads s(t) = r gets q*(L - r) instead of q*r. The graph is described in words because the engine has no figure support (book figure checked: straight line (0, 10) to (20, 0), i.e. q = 2 for L = 10). Every instance has T = L*q, so the rate is a whole number of seconds per metre and every answer is a whole number; r runs from 2 to L-2, so the ball is neither at the start nor at the bottom. 108 instances.
